description: MarsCraft is driven by our passion for space exploration, technology, and scientific innovation. Through this, we aim to build an interactive Mars exploration and survival platform using real NASA/USGS data, terrain analysis, geological mapping, and mission planning. We seek curious, driven teammates with interests or skills in programming, AI/ML, GIS, aerospace, astronomy, geology, and research who are eager to learn and collaborate.
summary:
MarsCraft is a web-based planning tool for a human Marswalk. It puts the data a crew would need for one EVA into a single map: where the terrain is gentle or steep, what a NASA rover actually found there, what the sky and space weather are doing, and which route is the best trade-off.
 
We built it for Jezero crater, the Mars 2020 landing region. It layers HRSC+MOLA elevation and derived slope, Viking, CTX and HiRISE imagery, THEMIS thermal mosaics, CRISM mineral signatures, Perseverance's 45 km traverse and Navcam frames, MEDA weather and DONKI space-weather predictions. An A* planner compares Shortest, Balanced and Cautious routes between science stops and runs six pre-EVA checks (time budget, daylight, space weather, slope, rover ground truth, data gaps).
 
It matters because a first Mars crew will walk in suits, with limited hours and little margin for error. Most NASA map tools are built for regional views. MarsCraft works at the scale of a single excursion and is honest about uncertainty: missing data is shown as "unknown", never as "safe". We also cross-checked the terrain model against Perseverance's own measurements.
details:
What it does

MarsCraft is a three-workspace web app that shares one map and one mission state:

  1. Mission overview. Loads the demo scenario (Jezero Delta Margin EVA), shows the current conditions (daylight, season, space weather) and lists every NASA dataset behind the view.
  2. Mars explorer. Switchable layers: Viking, CTX (6 m) and HiRISE (25 cm) imagery; THEMIS day and night infrared; CRISM minerals; the Perseverance traverse; elevation, slope and slope class. Clicking any point gives its elevation, slope class and the nearest rover stop with the rover's own elevation and tilt. Where a point of interest has one, a "what you may see" image (HiRISE or Mastcam-Z) is shown, and live Perseverance Navcam frames can be requested for the nearest stop.
  3. Mission planner. The crew picks a start, science waypoints and a destination, and the planner returns three routes. It shows an elevation and slope profile that traces the route on the map, a plain-language comparison of the routes, six pre-EVA checks, a radiation order-of-magnitude note, and GeoJSON and text exports.

Demo mission. An 8-hour EVA from a habitat near Octavia E. Butler Landing to the western delta, with 2 hours of science at the delta, then back. The Cautious route is 11.28 km, takes 7.6 h (5.6 h walking at an assumed 2 km/h plus 2 h of science) and passes 4 of 6 checks with 2 cautions (thin 0.4 h time margin and a CME arrival predicted near the period). The route's maximum grid slope is 2.5°.

Mission OverviewExplorer with DEM , slope class , elevation profile and rover traversePlanner with Cautious route and slope profilePre-EVA checks and route comparison

How it works

  • Terrain. USGS's blended HRSC+MOLA DEM (200 m) is cropped to 74–79°E, 17–22°N and block-averaged to about 590 m cells (494 × 494). Slope is computed with Horn's 3×3 method using real metre distances per row (latitude-corrected). Cells are classed Low (<5°), Moderate (5–15°), High (≥15°) or Unknown. Unknown is a separate class and is never merged into Low.
  • Routing. A* over an 8-connected grid with a great-circle heuristic. Step cost is length × (1 + (slope / S0)²), (where S0 is slope scale) with a penalty for unknown slope and a hard exclusion above a maximum slope. Three profiles (Shortest, Balanced, Cautious) are solved for every plan. To compare them fairly, every route is re-scored with the Balanced parameters ("reference cost"), and the explanation text is generated from those numbers.
  • Conditions. Season (Ls) and day length are computed for today with the Mars24 algorithm. DONKI WSA-ENLIL runs are filtered for Mars arrivals, de-duplicated and turned into Quiet / Watch / Alert. A "Quiet" reading from stale data is shown as Unknown. Weather and space-weather feeds are labelled live, cached or offline snapshot.
  • Pre-EVA checks. Pass, caution, flagged or unknown for: EVA time budget, daylight window, space weather, slope on route, rover ground truth and terrain data gaps. A missing input is never counted as a pass.
  • Offline behaviour. DEM, slope, CRISM figure, rover traverse and the feed snapshots are bundled with the app, so it still works without network access. Only the Trek imagery tiles and live Navcam frames need a connection.

Validation (what we checked, and what we found)

  • Code. 36 automated tests pass (Vitest). They cover slope on analytic planes, latitude scaling, missing-data propagation, routing, and season and day length checked against the Mars 2020 MEDA feed (Ls within 1°, day length within 3 minutes).
  • DEM resolution sensitivity. The 3×3 block-average reproduces the production DEM exactly. Coarse and fine slopes differ by a mean of 1.1° (median 0.73°, 95th percentile 3.5°). Threshold disagreement is 9.6% at 5° and 1.7% at 15°. See the figure below.
  • Against Perseverance. Across 554 end-of-drive stops (53 grid cells), grid elevation agrees with the rover's to about 27 m RMSE. Rover tilt exceeded grid slope at 80% of stops. This shows how much walking-scale relief a 590 m grid averages away, which is why rover tilt is reported as a separate check and "no high-slope cells" is not presented as "gentle ground".
DEM slope resolution-sensitivity validation

Benefits and intended impact

  • Puts terrain, science targets, conditions and route trade-offs in one view, so a crew does not have to switch between global viewers.
  • Safety-first design: unknown means unknown, three transparent cost profiles, time, daylight and space-weather checks, and a stated list of what is and is not modelled.
  • Grounded in what a rover actually measured. The Perseverance traverse and tilt data act as a reality check on orbital data.
  • Intended impact: a working pattern for pre-EVA planning that mission designers and educators can extend to other sites, since the data pipeline and planner are separate from the Jezero scenario.

Creativity

  • Rover-as-ground-truth: the app compares orbital slope with what Perseverance felt at 554 stops and reports where the model under-calls hazard.
  • Honest-uncertainty design: "Unknown" class, stale-data demotion, archived-feed labelling and a "modelled / not modelled" panel.
  • A "what you may see" view (HiRISE and Mastcam-Z) at science stops, plus live Navcam frames for the nearest rover stop, so a crew knows what to expect on arrival.
  • Fair route comparison on a common reference cost, with generated plain-language explanations.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: slope limits, unknown terrain, daylight, time budget, space weather and a cosmic-ray dose estimate.
  • Suited mobility and logistics: walking speed, science time, round trip back to the habitat (walk-back reachability layer).
  • Data honesty: resolution limits, approximate CRISM georeferencing, the MEDA public feed stopping in April 2024, and DONKI predicting CME arrival rather than dose.
  • Reliability: offline snapshots, caching, shareable URLs for each workspace, keyboard shortcuts, mobile layout.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages / frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, Vite 7, Leaflet, Vitest. No backend.
  • Data preparation: Python (rasterio, NumPy) for DEM processing and validation; Node.js scripts for NASA context snapshots and rover cross-checks.
  • Hardware: none beyond a standard laptop and a browser.
  • Development approach: the code was written with AI coding assistants (GitHub Copilot agent mostly with Claude, ChatGPT and Grok) and reviewed and tested by the team. The scientific core lives in src/core with no UI dependencies and has unit and integration tests.

Known limitations

MarsCraft is a research and planning prototype, not operational navigation software. Cost parameters are planning assumptions, not validated mobility data. The ~590 m grid cannot see boulders or small craters. Imagery, thermal and mineral layers are visual context and do not enter route cost. The CRISM figure is an approximately georeferenced publication image. Radiation figures come from Curiosity at Gale, not Jezero.
